https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-14-killed-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OoLM Prefer DW on Google The strike hit a crowded train platform during the morning rush hour Image: State Emergency Service of Ukraine/Handout/REUTERS Advertisement The death toll from a Russian drone attack on a passenger train which was stopped at a station in Dnipro in eastern Ukraine on Thursday morning has risen to 14, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed. According to Ukrainian state railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia , a jet-powered drone struck a crowded platform on which people were waiting to board a regional train to Zaporizhzhia, about a two-hour journey to the south. "Despite an increased threat warning, people were on the platform," the company said. Ukraine's air force said it had intercepted three drones in the daytime attack, but that a fourth evaded its defences and hit the station. In images circulating on social media, bodies could be seen strewn across a train station platform, with police officers kneeling beside them. "Russia is deliberately hunting civilians: on trains, ​at stations, in residential buildings," Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretskyi said. "There ​is no ‌justification for this terror, and there never can be." Dnipro city mayor Borys Filatov also confirmed the incident, which he called a "tragedy." Zelenskyy issues veiled Trump criticism after 'horrific' attack Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the attack "horrific" and demanded international action from Kyiv's allies. "Sanctions against Moscow and its war machine must not be eased for as long as this Russian war continues," he said. "How many such terrorist strikes has Russia carried out against our people since sanctions were lifted on some Russian oligarchs and energy sector, instead of de-escalating?" he asked, referring to a deal struck this month between US President Donald Trump and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin which saw some sanctions on Russia eased and the release of Russian diesel stocks onto global markets. French President Emmanuel Macron expressed his "deep concern" that Russia continues to "opt for escalation" by targeting civilians. "In this context, we must aim for much more than a localized ceasefire — such as the one recently negotiated for Oleshky ," the French president said on social media, describing Moscow’s rejection of "all proposals to that end" as "intolerable." "Together, we must redouble our efforts to achieve a just and lasting peace and bring Russia to the negotiating table," he said. "These are deliberate strikes against civilians, brazen in their cruelty, and the Russians are carrying them out right as the humanitarian operation in Oleshky is unfolding," continued Zelenskyy. "Russia's signals are clear – they want the war to continue, and everyone around the world must still work very hard to achieve major de-escalation through strong steps and appropriate pressure on the aggressor." DW witnesses Ukrainian train evacuation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video How Russia targets Ukrainian trains Russia has been targeting Ukrainian trains and stations since day one of the full-scale invasion in February 2022 , destroying hundreds of locomotives and killing railway workers and passengers. Faced with an increasing number of Russian drone attacks, Ukrainian trains began large-scale passenger evacuations this year — often while trains are already mid-journey. In September alone, more than 5,800 trains had to be evacuated due to the threat of strikes, Ukrzaliznytsia told the AFP news agency. Most evacuations take place in regions near the front line, in the south and east of the country: in Odesa, Dnipro and Zaporizhzhia. When a potential Russian strike is detected, the train comes to a halt and passengers are required to leave their carriages and wait at a safe distance until the danger has passed. With commercial air travel in Ukraine shut down due to the war, the country's vast railway network has become essential for transporting people and goods, as well as for entering and leaving Ukraine. Ukraine: More Russian attacks Also on Thursday, authorities reported at least five other fatalities resulting from other Russian attacks across Ukraine. A strike on the city center of Chernigiv, north of Kyiv, killed two 15-year-old girls and wounded more than a dozen, according to the head of the city's military administration. Elsewhere, a drone slammed into a multi-storey residential building in the central city of Kremenchuk, killing two and wounding several — including a six-year-old. https://www.dw.com/en/germany-2-arrested.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PufT Prefer DW on Google The suspects are accused of plotting an attack against Cologne's synagogue Image: Christoph Hardt/Panama Pictures/picture alliance Advertisement Germany 's federal prosecutor's office on Thursday said it had ordered the arrest of two Iraqi citizens in Germany who are believed to be members of a pro- Iranian terrorist group. It identified the men as Mostafa Al-R. and Ameer J., and said that they were arrested in Heidelberg in Baden-Württemberg in the southwest, and in Cologne , several hours' drive to the north. Officers from Germany's federal criminal police force carried out the arrests. Prosecutors also announced searches and raids of 17 sites in total across three separate states, saying these were ongoing. After two suspects were arrested, Hendrik Wüst, the premier of North Rhine-Westphalia , thanked the security agencies for their vigilance and dedication. "Protecting Jewish life is our shared responsibility," he wrote on X. "Jewish life must be able to flourish freely and safely in our country. Anyone who attacks it attacks us all," Wüst added. What accusations do the men face? Prosecutors said the two men were "strongly suspected" of membership in a domestic terrorist organization. They said that Mostafa Al-R. wa an associate of a man in the US known as Mohammad Al-Saadi, who is accused of setting up a group with the acronym HAYI (Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiyya) that is thought to be "responsible for a series of attacks against US, Israeli and Jewish institutions in Europe from March 2026," in the aftermath of the outbreak of Donald Trump's war with Iran . Mostafa Al-R. and Al-Saadi allegedly "founded a separate organization to prepare and carry out further attacks in Germany and Europe at the end of 2025." Police vehicles were spotted at the Federal Court of Justice on Thursday, apparently bringing the suspects to a hearing on being held in investigative detention Image: Rene Piebe/PR-Video/dpa/picture alliance Prosecutors say Ameer J. joined this group. It gathered funds and "recruited several external people to carry out explosive attacks." "On the group's orders, unknown assailants headed on two consecutive nights in late March 2026 — presumably with explosives — to synagogues in Cologne and in one other European city," prosecutors wrote. "The plan was, for reasons as yet unknown, ultimately not carried out." Prosecutors said that intelligence behind the arrests could be traced back to the federal domestic intelligence agency , the BfV. More than 250 police officers from various forces were part of Thursday's operation. Both suspects were expected to appear before judges later on Thursday for a decision on them being placed in investigative detention. One other person is being sought as part of the investigation, with several others not currently suspected of criminal offenses affected by it. What happened during the series of antisemitic attacks in Europe in spring? The stated date for the plot to attack Cologne's synagogue, late March this year, would have roughly coincided with a series of crimes in Europe targeting Jewish people or institutions in the weeks after the outbreak of war with Iran. These included an explosion in front of Liege synagogue in Belgium on March 9 , which caused property damage but no injuries. Police in the Netherlands investigated a fire at Rotterdam's synagogue a few days later . An explosive device was set off outside a Jewish school in Amsterdam soon after , prompting heightened security across the Netherlands. In London, a Jewish ambulance service was targeted in arson attacks in March , not long before two Jewish men were stabbed in broad daylight in what investigators treated as a likely act of terrorism. Several months later, in September, police in Wuppertal in Germany arrested an Afghan national on suspicion of trying to set a fire at the city's synagogue.
